lesson.title: The Angle That Isn't Straight: Bent Molecules and Why Water Works
lesson.summary: Bent geometry appears when one or two lone pairs crowd a central atom's remaining bonding pairs out of a straight or symmetric line, producing water's iconic V shape and giving it the polarity that makes it such an effective solvent.
lesson.body:
Bent geometry is not a single, fixed shape the way linear or tetrahedral geometry are. It is a naming outcome that shows up in two different situations, both of which share the same underlying cause: lone pairs occupying some of the positions in an electron geometry that would otherwise have been fully symmetric if every domain were a bonding pair. The word bent simply describes what remains once you look only at where the atoms sit, since the lone pairs themselves are invisible in the final drawn shape but are still very much present and still very much repelling their neighbors.

The first way bent geometry arises is from a steric number of three with one lone pair, written as AX2E in shorthand, where the electron geometry is trigonal planar. Sulfur dioxide, SO2, is the standard example. Sulfur has three electron domains, two bonding domains to oxygen and one lone pair, giving a trigonal planar electron geometry. Naming only the three atoms, sulfur and two oxygens, produces a bent molecular geometry with a bond angle of about 119 degrees, just slightly less than the ideal 120 degrees of a full trigonal planar arrangement, because the lone pair pushes the two oxygen bonding domains a bit closer together than they would otherwise sit.

The second, more commonly taught way bent geometry arises is from a steric number of four with two lone pairs, written as AX2E2, where the electron geometry is tetrahedral. Water, H2O, is the essential example here. Oxygen has four electron domains: two bonding pairs to the two hydrogen atoms and two lone pairs. This directly connects to the earlier discussion of lone pairs, since it is precisely because oxygen carries two lone pairs, rather than the one lone pair seen in ammonia, that water's shape and angle differ so much from ammonia's.

Naming only the three atoms in water, hydrogen, oxygen, and hydrogen, gives a bent molecular geometry, but the measured H to O to H bond angle is about 104.5 degrees, noticeably smaller than the 109.5 degree angle of an ideal tetrahedral arrangement. This compression happens because lone pairs are held by only one nucleus and spread into a broader region of space than bonding pairs do, so their repulsion pushes neighboring domains closer together. With two lone pairs instead of one, water experiences even more of this compressive repulsion than ammonia does, which is exactly why its angle drops further below the ideal value.

This bent, non symmetric shape is the direct reason water is such a strongly polar molecule and such an effective solvent. If water were linear, the two O to H bond dipoles would point in exactly opposite directions and cancel out completely, just as they do in linear carbon dioxide. Because water's molecular geometry is bent rather than linear, those two bond dipoles do not cancel, and the molecule carries a substantial net dipole moment. That polarity is what allows water to dissolve salts and other polar substances, and it is what enables water molecules to form hydrogen bonds with one another, a property responsible for water's unusually high boiling point and its behavior as the near universal solvent of biology and chemistry.
